title: Why one side of this mountain is a forest — and the other is a desert
subtitle: Mount Hood / Cascade Range / Oregon High Desert
deck: Stand on the wet western Cascades and the land feels endless green. Cross the range and the air thins into sage, dust, and open sky. The mountain is not magic — it is a barrier written into the weather.
shortDescription: Pacific moisture, a mountain barrier, and the quiet geometry of a rain shadow.
seoTitle: Why Mount Hood Is Forest on One Side and Desert on the Other — Deep Forest Dispatch
metaDescription: Explore the Cascade rain shadow around Mount Hood: orographic lifting, cooling air, and why Oregon’s west is wet while the high desert stays dry.

hero.alt: Cascade volcanoes and surrounding terrain seen from orbit

blocks.html: West of the Cascades, moist Pacific air feeds temperate forests, deep moss, and frequent cloud. East of the range, the land opens into the Oregon High Desert and Columbia Plateau country — bright, dry, and often wind-scoured.

Mount Hood is one of the Cascade volcanoes that make this divide visible. The mountain does not “create” two climates by itself; it stands inside a larger barrier system. Still, from trailheads to satellite views, Hood is a memorable place to feel the difference.

blocks.alt: Side-by-side atmospheric illustration of wet western slopes and dry eastern high desert
blocks.caption: Same latitude band, different water story: wet western slopes versus dry eastern rain-shadow country.
blocks.credit: Waypoint Studio educational illustration for Deep Forest Dispatch

blocks.html: Follow the Cascade Range north–south through Oregon. On the west: Portland, the Willamette Valley, and forested Cascades foothills. On the east: high desert basins, sagebrush steppe, and agricultural valleys that depend on irrigation and snowmelt.

blocks.caption: Mount Hood and the Cascade crest between wet western Oregon and drier country to the east.

blocks.alt: Perspective view of Portland, Mount Hood, and the Columbia River Gorge
blocks.caption: Portland, Mount Hood, and the Columbia River Gorge in a NASA perspective view — west-side moisture country meeting a towering Cascade landmark.

blocks.html: Prevailing winds in this region often carry moist air inland from the Pacific. When that air meets the Cascades, it cannot easily continue at the same altitude. The range forces the flow upward.
That forced climb is the start of the rain-shadow story. Geography becomes weather: a wall of rock rearranges where water falls.
Meteorologists call this orographic lifting: terrain pushes an air mass upslope. As the parcel rises, pressure drops and the air expands.
Think of it as a ramp. The Pacific delivers the moisture; the Cascades supply the ramp; physics does the rest.
Expanding air cools. Cooler air holds less water vapor. When cooling reaches the dew point, water vapor condenses into cloud droplets — and, often, precipitation.
On the windward Cascades, that process can be relentless: orographic clouds, rain, snow at elevation, and forests that live on the result.

blocks.alt: Atmospheric illustration of misty western Cascade forest slopes
blocks.caption: Windward slopes: rising air, cooling, condensation, and a landscape organized around water.

blocks.html: After releasing moisture on the climb, the air continues over the crest and descends on the lee side. Descending air compresses and warms. Warmer air can hold more moisture relative to what remains — so clouds thin and rainfall drops.
That leeward dryness is the rain shadow. East of the Cascades, the high desert is not an accident of aesthetics. It is the other half of the same atmospheric transaction that greens the west.

blocks.alt: Diagram of orographic lifting and rain shadow across a mountain barrier
Atmospheric illustration of Oregon high desert east of the Cascades
blocks.caption: Leeward country: brighter, drier, and shaped by air that already spent much of its water on the climb.

blocks.html: From orbit, Cascade volcanoes puncture cloud decks and snowfields. Valleys west of the crest often look softer and greener; basins to the east read as more open and arid. The pattern is regional — Mount Hood is one vivid chapter in a longer Cascade story.

blocks.alt: Earth observation of Cascade terrain from the International Space Station
blocks.caption: ISS Earth observation across Cascade terrain — a reminder that climate contrasts can be geographic, not mysterious.

blocks.html: If this contrast made you want to read conditions before a trip west of the Cascades — or plan a photograph in shifting mountain light — Waypoint’s outdoor tools are built for that next step.
